primaryText: If you want to go to Harlem, you should / have to take the A train.
context: On a subway platform the speaker notices a stranger who appears lost and might be on his way to Harlem; as it happens the stranger wants to go to Hoboken, accessible only by the PATH train.
comment: The Harlem sentence, after Sæbø; conveys that taking the A train is necessary for going to Harlem. True in the Hoboken scenario, `HobokenScenario.anankastic_harlem`.

primaryText: If you intend to go to Harlem, you should / have to take the A train.
comment: Intention predicates give the same interpretation; intending entails effectively preferring.

primaryText: If you are planning to go to Harlem, you should / have to take the A train.
If your goal is to go to Harlem, you should / have to take the A train.
If you want to eat chocolate, you should try thinking about something else.
comment: Advice on how to avoid eating chocolate: want reports a mere desire and the modal is teleological, (105).

primaryText: If you want to go to Harlem, you can take the PATH train.
context: On a subway platform the speaker notices a stranger who appears lost and might be on his way to Harlem; as it happens the stranger wants to go to Hoboken, accessible only by the PATH train.
comment: Intuitively false in the Hoboken scenario, as Condoravdi and Lauer predict, `HobokenScenario.not_possibility_path`; Sæbø's augmented ordering source predicts it true, `HobokenScenario.saebo_path`.

primaryText: If you want to go to Hoboken, you have to / should take the PATH train.
context: On a subway platform the speaker notices a stranger who appears lost and might be on his way to Harlem; as it happens the stranger wants to go to Hoboken, accessible only by the PATH train.
comment: True together with the Harlem sentence in the Hoboken scenario, `HobokenScenario.anankastic_hoboken`.

primaryText: (In view of what he wants,) John should resign the game.
context: John and Bill are playing chess. John is by far the superior player, but Bill is good enough to draw out the game for a considerable amount of time, and competitive enough to not accept a draw. John hates to resign a game to an inferior player, but it is 3am, and he needs to go to bed. The only way to get out of the game quickly is to resign. The only way to win, of course, is to keep playing. He cannot make up his mind.
comment: Conflicting extrinsic preferences make one or both unconditional necessities false.

primaryText: (In view of what he wants,) John should not resign the game.
context: John and Bill are playing chess. John is by far the superior player, but Bill is good enough to draw out the game for a considerable amount of time, and competitive enough to not accept a draw. John hates to resign a game to an inferior player, but it is 3am, and he needs to go to bed. The only way to get out of the game quickly is to resign. The only way to win, of course, is to keep playing. He cannot make up his mind.

primaryText: If John wants to go to bed, he should resign.
context: John and Bill are playing chess. John is by far the superior player, but Bill is good enough to draw out the game for a considerable amount of time, and competitive enough to not accept a draw. John hates to resign a game to an inferior player, but it is 3am, and he needs to go to bed. The only way to get out of the game quickly is to resign. The only way to win, of course, is to keep playing. He cannot make up his mind.
comment: The conditional necessities are true in the same context, after Huitink.

primaryText: If John wants to win the game, he should not resign.
context: John and Bill are playing chess. John is by far the superior player, but Bill is good enough to draw out the game for a considerable amount of time, and competitive enough to not accept a draw. John hates to resign a game to an inferior player, but it is 3am, and he needs to go to bed. The only way to get out of the game quickly is to resign. The only way to win, of course, is to keep playing. He cannot make up his mind.

primaryText: If the only thing you want is to go to Harlem, you have to / should take the A train.
comment: Huitink's strong interpretation of the antecedent, too strong for near-anankastics.

primaryText: If you want to invite everyone to the dinner, your table has to seat at least 20 people.
comment: A necessary precondition rather than a means.

primaryText: If you want to travel to that place, you should / must get a vaccine to be safe.
comment: A strengthened goal: the internal antecedent joins the overt purpose clause; a near-anankastic with the anankastic parameter setting.

primaryText: If you want to travel to that place, you should / must get a vaccine.
comment: An implicit strengthened goal; the vaccine need not be a precondition for travelling. True with safety a second maximal preference, `VaccineScenario.should_vaccine`, false on the singleton construal, `VaccineScenario.not_should_vaccine_strong`.

primaryText: To travel there and be safe you should / must get a vaccine.
comment: The purpose construction the purpose-clause analyses reduce (29) to.

primaryText: If you want to go to Disneyworld, you must / should spend at least five days there.
comment: A near-anankastic about a teleological consequence of achieving the goal, with the same parameter setting as the Harlem sentence.

primaryText: To go to Disneyworld, you have to spend at least five days there.
comment: The same sentence as (99).

primaryText: If you went to Disneyworld, you would spend at least five days there.
context: You can only take three days off work, and this is mutually known.
comment: Von Stechow et al.'s similarity modal gives (31) and (37) the same truth conditions, but (31) can be true when (37) is false.

primaryText: If you want to use the exemption now, you must / will have to pay more taxes next year.
comment: A deontic near-anankastic: conveys that it is illegal to take the exemption now and not pay more taxes next year.

primaryText: If you want to go to the disaster area, you should go there quickly.
comment: A what-kind-of near-anankastic: the prejacent specializes the goal.

primaryText: To go to the disaster area, you should go there quickly.
If you want to buy a fancy dress, you should buy a well-made one.
comment: A what-kind-of near-anankastic: advice about what kind of fancy dress to buy.

primaryText: To buy a fancy dress, you should buy a well-made one.
If you bought a fancy dress, you would buy a well-made one.
comment: (40a) can be true when (42) is not, if the addressee lacks the funds for a well-made dress.

primaryText: If you take the exemption now, you must / will have to pay more taxes next year.
comment: Intuitively equivalent to (38), which suggests, misleadingly, that want is vacuous.

primaryText: If you buy a fancy dress, you should buy a well-made one.
comment: Intuitively equivalent to (40a).

primaryText: If you don't want to get a letter grade for the course, you don't have to take the exam.
comment: Due to Doris Penka; negation applies to want, so the conditional conditionalizes on indifference, which a vacuous want could not express.

primaryText: If you want to have sugar in your soup, you should ask the waiter.
comment: Hare's waiter case: want does not report a desire the agent has as a matter of psychological fact.

primaryText: If you want to have sugar in your soup, you should get tested for diabetes.
comment: Hare's diabetes case: want reports a desire the agent has as a matter of psychological fact.

primaryText: Do you want to play tennis? I want to, but I have to teach.
discourseSegments: Do you want to play tennis?
I want to, but I have to teach.
comment: Levinson's observation, after Davis: the two replies are not contradictory.

primaryText: Do you want to play tennis? No, I have to teach.
discourseSegments: Do you want to play tennis?
No, I have to teach.
comment: The no denies an effective preference.

primaryText: I want it to rain tomorrow so the picnic gets canceled, but I (also) want it to be sunny tomorrow so I can go hiking.
comment: Two known-incompatible wants asserted together; consistent on the mere-desire reading, since non-effective structures need not be consistent.

primaryText: John wants to move in with his girlfriend, but he also wants to keep living alone. He can't make up his mind.
John would like to move in with his girlfriend, but he would also like to keep living alone. He can't make up his mind.
comment: Coherent: attributes indecision.

primaryText: John intends to move in with his girlfriend, but he also intends to keep living alone.
comment: Printed unmarked; the prose says it sounds contradictory or attributes irrationality to John: two effective preferences the agent believes incompatible cannot both be maximal, `PreferenceStructure.Consistent.inter_inter_nonempty_of_mem_maxElts`.

primaryText: John would like to visit Paris this summer.
comment: Levinson's Paris and Rome case: (56a) and (56b) can be true without (58) if John disprefers the expense of both; on the effective reading that third preference excludes the first two being effective, `no_third_effective`.

primaryText: John would like to visit Rome this summer.
John would like to go to both Paris and Rome this summer.
John really wants to get the job, but he knows they won't hire him.
comment: A mere-desire reading; on the effective reading the half of the Heim and von Fintel presupposition that the agent does not believe the negation follows from realism, footnote 30.

primaryText: Nicholas wants to take a free trip on the Concorde.
comment: Asher's example, discussed by Levinson: paying for the trip would ruin Nicholas.

primaryText: Nicholas wants to take a trip on the Concorde.
comment: Levinson judges it false; the paper takes the judgment to rest on a success-oriented reading it rejects.

primaryText: John wants to get a poodle, so he wants to get a dog.
comment: Impeccable reasoning: want appears upward entailing, through a wide-scope sub-concept indefinite on the exact-match analysis.

primaryText: John wants to get a dog. So he would be happy to get a poodle.
comment: Printed unmarked; the prose says it is not valid reasoning on any construal: want is not downward entailing.

primaryText: If jaywalking is illegal here, then (in view of what the law provides) this dude has to pay a fine.
comment: After von Fintel and Iatridou: the antecedent is about the ordering source of the modal, so a restrictor analysis makes the conditional false when jaywalking is legal; Frank's double-modal structure (76b).

primaryText: If you lose your job, take a lower-paying one.
comment: Kaufmann and Schwager's conditional imperatives: consistent with (81b), against strengthening of the antecedent under a single imperative modal, `single_modal_strengthening`.

primaryText: But if you lose your job and have a comparable offer, don't take a lower-paying one.
If John gets a dog, he will have to pay more taxes.
context: Dog owners have to pay a special dog tax, but service dogs for the blind are exempt; John's eyesight is currently perfect and he does not currently have a dog.
comment: Defeasible obligation: dog owners pay a dog tax, service dogs for the blind are exempt, and John's eyesight is perfect.

primaryText: But if John loses his eyesight and gets a dog, he will not have to pay more taxes.
context: Dog owners have to pay a special dog tax, but service dogs for the blind are exempt; John's eyesight is currently perfect and he does not currently have a dog.
comment: Both true; a single-modal analysis would make losing one's eyesight against the law.

primaryText: If you want to get to the airport by noon, you should take the train.
context: Getting a ride is the most preferable way to get to the airport.
comment: An anankastic Sobel sequence; both true if the speaker is unwilling to drive when the trains run on time, `AirportScenario.should_train` and `AirportScenario.should_ride`, which no single modal ordered by the addressee's goals allows, `AirportScenario.not_single_modal`.

primaryText: If you want to get to the airport by noon and there is repair work on the tracks, I should give you a ride.
context: Getting a ride is the most preferable way to get to the airport.

primaryText: If Sophie had gone to the parade, she would have seen Pedro. But if Sophie had gone to the parade and been stuck behind a tall person, she would not have seen Pedro.
discourseSegments: If Sophie had gone to the parade, she would have seen Pedro.
But if Sophie had gone to the parade and been stuck behind a tall person, she would not have seen Pedro.
comment: A counterfactual Sobel sequence.

primaryText: If Sophie had gone to the parade and been stuck behind a tall person, she would not have seen Pedro. But if Sophie had gone to the parade, she would have seen Pedro.
discourseSegments: If Sophie had gone to the parade and been stuck behind a tall person, she would not have seen Pedro.
But if Sophie had gone to the parade, she would have seen Pedro.
comment: A reverse Sobel sequence, infelicitous; von Fintel and Gillies take it to favour a dynamic strict analysis.

primaryText: If you want to go to the airport and there are track repairs, you should take a taxi. But the taxi would be very expensive and track repairs are very unlikely, so if you want to go to the airport, you should take the Caltrain.
discourseSegments: If you want to go to the airport and there are track repairs, you should take a taxi.
But the taxi would be very expensive and track repairs are very unlikely, so if you want to go to the airport, you should take the Caltrain.
comment: A reverse anankastic Sobel sequence made felicitous by material about likelihood in between, which argues for a typicality ordering on the outer modal.

primaryText: I know John wants to go to Hoboken today, not to Harlem. But if he wants to go to Harlem today, he has to take the A train.
discourseSegments: I know John wants to go to Hoboken today, not to Harlem.
But if he wants to go to Harlem today, he has to take the A train.
comment: An indicative anankastic is out when the speaker knows of an incompatible effective preference: the antecedent is epistemically impossible and the conditional vacuously true, `Conditional.Restrictor.vacuous_conditional`. The paper prints "go Harlem".

primaryText: I know John wants to go to Hoboken today, not to Harlem. But if he wanted to go to Harlem today, he would have to take the A train.
discourseSegments: I know John wants to go to Hoboken today, not to Harlem.
But if he wanted to go to Harlem today, he would have to take the A train.

primaryText: If you want to go to Vladivostok, you have to take the Chinese train.
context: There are two trains to Vladivostok, one Russian and one Chinese. The Chinese train is much more comfortable.
comment: Von Stechow et al.'s case of a compatible salient preference: comfort stays in the ordering, so the conditional is true, `VladivostokScenario.haveTo_chinese_comfortFirst`; judged false if cost outranks comfort, `VladivostokScenario.not_haveTo_chinese_costFirst`.

primaryText: If you want to go to Harlem, you have to take the A train.
context: Two trains go to Harlem, and Ruud van Nistelrooij is on one of them; the addressee wants to meet him.
comment: Huitink's van Nistelrooij case: false with a strong modal even if the addressee effectively prefers meeting him; the strong/weak contrast is left open.

primaryText: If you want to go to Harlem, you should take the A train.
context: Two trains go to Harlem, and Ruud van Nistelrooij is on one of them; the addressee wants to meet him.
comment: True when the preference for meeting van Nistelrooij is salient, though not advice on how to get to Harlem.

primaryText: I know John wants to go to Hoboken today, not to Harlem. But to go to Harlem, he has to take the A train.
discourseSegments: I know John wants to go to Hoboken today, not to Harlem.
But to go to Harlem, he has to take the A train.
comment: Purpose constructions behave like conditionals: the indicative is out when the preference is known absent.

primaryText: I know John wants to go to Hoboken today, not to Harlem. But to go to Harlem, he would have to take the A train.
discourseSegments: I know John wants to go to Hoboken today, not to Harlem.
But to go to Harlem, he would have to take the A train.

primaryText: To go to Disneyworld, you have to spend at least five days there.
comment: Purpose constructions exclude teleological-consequence readings, since the prejacent cannot be subsequent to the goal; the same sentence as (35a).

primaryText: To go to Harlem, you have to stay on this platform.
comment: Purpose constructions are compatible with mere necessary preconditions.

primaryText: For us to invite everyone to dinner, your table has to seat at least 20.
If you want to go to Harlem, you should / have to take the A train.
context: The speaker knows that a deadly virus has just been set free in Harlem, and that anyone who goes there is likely to be infected. As far as the speaker knows, the addressee is unaware of this.
comment: Printed unmarked; intuitions are not clear-cut, but the paper argues the sentence is not true on the anankastic reading. A variant of the virus scenario of Lauer and Condoravdi 2014: the addressee is unaware of a conflict with staying alive.

primaryText: Well, if he wants to go to Harlem right now, he has to / should take the A train.
discourseSegments: A: Why is he doing that?
B: Well, if he wants to go to Harlem right now, he has to / should take the A train.
context: A and B are watching a disaster movie in which a virus is set free in Harlem. After a scene of people dropping dead in the street, the movie cuts to the hero, C, who is going about his day in Manhattan, oblivious to the outbreak. C is studying the schedule for the A train.
comment: Felicitous on a subjective construal of the outer modal that takes only the facts known to the hero into account, after Egan, Hawthorne and Weatherson.

primaryText: If you want to drop out of school, you should talk to the guidance counselor. He will help you with the necessary paper work.
discourseSegments: If you want to drop out of school, you should talk to the guidance counselor.
He will help you with the necessary paper work.
comment: The continuation brings out the anankastic reading.

primaryText: If you want to drop out of school, you should talk to the guidance counselor. So we can figure out what makes you unhappy, and find ways to address the issues.
discourseSegments: If you want to drop out of school, you should talk to the guidance counselor.
So we can figure out what makes you unhappy, and find ways to address the issues.
comment: Want gets the mere-desire reading, as if the antecedent were if you are unhappy in school; the modal is hearer- or speaker-teleological.

primaryText: If you want to drop out of school, you should talk to the guidance counselor. Maybe he can convince you to change your mind.
discourseSegments: If you want to drop out of school, you should talk to the guidance counselor.
Maybe he can convince you to change your mind.
comment: Want gets the effective reading but the modal is speaker-teleological.

primaryText: To use the exemption now, you must / will have to pay more taxes next year.
comment: (38) has no purpose-clause paraphrase.

primaryText: If you want to win the lottery, you must / will have to pay more taxes next year.
comment: The contextual assumption behind deontic near-anankastics, that an effective preference for the content is actualized, fails, so want is not vacuous and the sentence can only be true if merely wanting to win raised one's taxes.

primaryText: If you want to win the lottery, you have to buy a ticket.
comment: A proper anankastic needs no assumption that the preference will be realized.

primaryText: If you want to go to Harlem, you have to breathe.
comment: Printed unmarked; the prose says (110) sounds odd though true, with von Fintel and Iatridou: the consequent holds unconditionally, so the conditional is hard to justify.

primaryText: If you want to go to Harlem, you have to be a person.
comment: Printed unmarked; sounds odd though true, like (110a).

primaryText: If you want to go to Harlem, you have to wait on this platform.
comment: A partial precondition informative enough to warrant assertion.

primaryText: If you'd like to go to Harlem, you have to take the A train.
comment: Weatherson's weak antecedents, via von Fintel and Iatridou 2006: the desire predicate cannot target effective preferences, so no anankastic construal arises and the sentence is false unless the context treats any such desire as acted upon.

primaryText: If you'd care to go to Harlem, you have to take the A train.
If you're inclined to go to Harlem, you have to take the A train.
If you're thinking about going to Harlem, you have to take the A train.
If you think you might (want to) go to Harlem, you have to take the A train.
